summary: FLARE+ turns NASA's scattered microgravity combustion record into evidence that mission designers can trust and query. We brought together 1,990 tests from 24 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigations, 352 publications and 695 NASA technical reports into one open, searchable database. Then we went beyond NASA's tables: by mining raw sensor recordings, video and images, we recovered flame outcomes for 943 ACME tests (93.8% agreement with NASA's labels), 139 BASS flame episodes and Saffire spread rates within a few percent of published values. Along the way we found a mis-scaled pressure formula and a table-versus-paper disagreement. Validated models predict ignition and self-extinction and give a simple formula for droplet burning rate. An interactive dashboard and assistant link every number to its source file and trust level. They rank investigations by relevance to fire prevention, detection and suppression in spacecraft cabins, lunar habitats and spacesuits, and suggest the most informative next ISS experiment. Because fire in a sealed spacecraft leaves the crew nowhere to escape, decisions need evidence that is transparent, can be reproduced and is open about its uncertainty. That is what we built.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

FLARE+ turns NASA’s scattered microgravity combustion record into traceable, queryable engineering evidence. Automated Python pipelines unify 24 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations, NTRS technical reports, and 352 journal publications into an open SQLite database containing 1,990 tests and 7,924 full-text pages. Going beyond pre-tabulated spreadsheets, we mined raw ACME sensor telemetry, BASS flame videos, and Saffire spacecraft burn imagery to extract previously untabulated metrics—recovering flame outcomes for 943 tests (93.8% agreement with NASA labels) and flame spread rates within a few percent of published benchmarks, while uncovering a mis-scaled pressure formula in existing records. On top of this dataset, machine learning models built with scikit-learn and PyTorch (validated strictly by test day) predict ignition and self-extinction boundaries, map flammability regimes across oxygen and pressure, translate microgravity flow data to Lunar (0.16g) and Martian (0.38g) gravity equivalents, and use a Gaussian Process to recommend the most informative next ISS flight experiment. Users explore these results through a dual-mode JavaScript web interface (a scenario-driven Insight workbench for mission planners and a full Researcher explorer) paired with a Claude-powered assistant that grounds every number in its primary source file and one of six explicit trust levels.

Benefits & Intended Impact

In a sealed spacecraft, lunar habitat, or EVA spacesuit, crews cannot evacuate a fire, and conventional Earth-based fire codes fail in low-gravity, oxygen-enriched atmospheres. FLARE+ reduces mission risk and experimental cost by allowing aerospace engineers to instantly audit which flight hardware and fuel tests match a target cabin atmosphere, avoid dangerous out-of-distribution extrapolations, and prioritize high-value ISS tests instead of repeating redundant burns. Back on Earth, mapping microgravity flame limits directly informs safer lithium-ion battery thermal runaway containment, hyperbaric oxygen chamber protocols, and cleanroom fire suppression.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

    • Data & Signal Mining: Python, SQLite, OpenCV / image-processing pipelines, and custom telemetry parsers for raw ACME, BASS, and Saffire files.
    • Machine Learning & Modeling: PyTorch, scikit-learn, NumPy/SciPy (Gaussian Process boundary modeling and per-day cross-validation).
    • Web Application & AI Integration: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, SVG data visualizations, Render cloud hosting, and the Anthropic Claude API with deterministic source-citation checks.Creativity & Key Engineering Considerations

Creativity Key and Engineering Considerations

Rather than building a generic RAG chatbot over static tables, our project treats missing data and physical uncertainty as first-class citizens: mining raw sensor signals to recover missing outcomes, displaying oxygen-only runs on dedicated plot axes instead of discarding them, letting the AI assistant drive the exact same interactive views users click, and openly documenting failed modeling approaches. Throughout development, our team prioritized scientific rigor, full reproducibility, strict refusal to extrapolate outside tested Oxygen/pressure bounds, and transparent handling of real-world data limitations—such as uncalibrated sensor voltages and the lack of long-duration partial-gravity flight data.
